record.narrative: Initial exploration should target established oncogenic dependencies and synthetic-lethal relationships in this lung cancer screen dataset. Because dependency scores are more negative when dependency is stronger, most oncogene-addiction hypotheses are written with direction -1. KRAS-mutant cells are expected to show stronger KRAS dependence; EGFR-, ERBB2-, and BRAF-mutant/amplified cells are expected to show stronger dependence on their corresponding receptors or kinases. KEAP1 loss may activate NRF2/NFE2L2 signaling and increase NFE2L2 dependence. ARID1A loss is a classic candidate for SMARCA2 synthetic lethality. TP53 loss is hypothesized to reduce dependence on p53-restraining regulators such as MDM2 and USP7; therefore those claims are written with direction +1, expecting exposed TP53-loss cells to have less negative dependency scores than TP53-intact cells. MYC amplification may increase transcriptional and proteostatic burden, leading to stronger POLR2A dependency. MSI-high cancers have a known selective WRN dependency. Finally, higher serum may activate growth-factor and STAT3-associated signaling, so high serum exposure is initially compared with low serum for STAT3 dependency. These comparisons are registered as unresolved until effect sizes and uncertainty are observed.

Run the full round-1 discovery panel of 12 registered comparisons to obtain initial effect estimates, confidence intervals, and cell counts for the prioritized biological associations. These analyses cover oncogenic addiction markers (KRAS, EGFR, ERBB2, BRAF), pathway-driven dependencies (KEAP1/NFE2L2, MYC/POLR2A, MSI/WRN, ARID1A/SMARCA2), TP53-loss effects on MDM2/USP7, and a culture-condition serum contrast for STAT3.

The round-1 discovery evidence supports two strong and clinically meaningful dependency associations. MSI-high cells show a large increase in WRN dependency, and TP53-loss cells show a large reduction in USP7 dependency; both 95% intervals are far from zero and well beyond the approximate 10% relative effect scale for these outcomes, so H10 and H11 are accepted as dataset-specific findings. The KRAS, ERBB2, BRAF, ARID1A-SMARCA2, MYC-POLR2A, and MDM2 associations were mostly small and compatible with no clinically meaningful difference. H6 was especially notable because the signed effect was opposite to the anticipated direction by a very large magnitude; the original KEAP1-loss claim that NFE2L2 dependency would be stronger is therefore rejected, while I registered a reversed claim for the observed opposite association. EGFR amplification H3 is borderline: the signed estimate is near the 10% threshold and the interval is almost entirely positive but narrowly includes zero, making this the most useful independent validation target. H1, H4, H8, and H12 are left unresolved because their upper interval bounds still cross a plausible meaningful effect despite non-significant point estimates. No conclusions are drawn about causality or external generalizability; these are associations in the supplied discovery dataset.

The new validation for H3 does not support acceptance. The original discovery suggested EGFR amplification may be associated with stronger EGFR dependency (signed effect +0.025; raw difference would be more negative), and its lower bound was very close to zero. However, the independent validation estimate is opposite in sign and essentially null (+/- adjusted interval -0.050 to +0.038). Because the validation interval is adjusted and broad, it neither confirms a clinically meaningful positive effect nor establishes a strong negative effect. The combined evidence therefore remains too ambiguous to accept or reject H3, but the most likely interpretation is that any overall EGFR-amplification effect is small, unstable, or context-dependent. I keep H3 active because H14 can test whether the effect differs by KRAS mutation status, which is biologically plausible given mutual exclusivity and pathway bypass between EGFR and KRAS alterations.

The reverse NFE2L2 claim H13 should now be accepted. The direct evidence is extraordinarily strong and precise: signed estimate +0.796 with a 95% interval +0.776 to +0.816, far beyond the approximate 10% relative threshold. In raw biological terms, KEAP1-loss cells appear to have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency than KEAP1-intact cells, which is the opposite of the initially anticipated direction but is exactly what the data show. This is a dataset-specific association; it does not prove that KEAP1 loss causes reduced NFE2L2 dependency, nor that it will generalize to other cell lines or screening platforms. I keep H13 active so that it can be considered for independent validation, given that the original anticipated direction failed and the magnitude is biologically surprising.

Overall, the strongest supported findings in this supplied dataset remain: MSI-high cells have much stronger WRN dependency, TP53-loss cells have much weaker USP7 dependency, and KEAP1-loss cells have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. Negative or not-supported findings include KRAS-mutation effects on RIT1, BRAF-V600E effects on BRAF dependency, ARID1A-loss effects on SMARCA2 dependency, and MYC-amplification effects on POLR2A dependency. EGFR amplification, KRAS dependency by KRAS mutation, ERBB2 amplification, TP53-loss effects on MDM2 dependency, and serum effects on STAT3 dependency remain uncertain. The most informative next analyses are to run H13 if validation can be requested, then the registered follow-up interactions H14-H19 and the KRAS adenocarcinoma subgroup H16.

Registered round-2 comparisons fall into three scientifically useful categories. First, refinements test whether accepted or borderline associations are context-dependent rather than universal: EGFR amplification in adenocarcinoma, KRAS dependency modified by STK11 loss, WRN dependency modified by mutation burden, USP7/TP53-loss association checked against Cas9 activity, STAT3 serum contrast checked in high IFN-gamma state, and reverse KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 association checked in KRAS-mutant context. Second, a new synthetic-lethality candidate tests SMARCA4 loss rather than ARID1A loss for SMARCA2 dependency, since ARID1A loss alone was not informative in round 1. Third, broad outcome coverage probes MYC amplification against DHX9 and RPL11, plausible transcription/ribosome-stress dependencies. No assessments are due at explore. These are dataset-specific hypotheses; strong results may support acceptance after appraisal, but causality and generalizability remain separate issues.

Selected the 12 most informative currently untested comparisons. This panel combines follow-up on unresolved accepted/borderline findings with targeted new hypotheses. For EGFR amplification, H14 tests whether failure of the overall effect is due to KRAS-mutant context; H15/H20 probe ARID1A-loss by SMARCA4-loss context and SMARCA4-loss main effect for SMARCA2 dependency, a stronger synthetic-lethality hypothesis than ARID1A loss alone. For KRAS dependency, H16/H22 test whether the borderline main effect is restricted to adenocarcinoma or modified by STK11 loss. For the accepted USP7-TP53 loss association, H18 tests biological effect modification by MTAP loss and H23 tests technical robustness across higher Cas9 activity. For the accepted reverse NFE2L2-KEAP1 loss association, H19/H28 test effect modification by TP53 and KRAS co-alteration. H25 explores whether the borderline serum effect on STAT3 is present in a high IFN-gamma state. H26/H27 broaden outcome coverage to DHX9 and RPL11 as plausible MYC-amplification-associated transcription/ribosome-stress dependencies, after the POLR2A association was not supported. No assessment is due because these analyses are newly requested.

The strongest new result is H20: SMARCA4 loss is associated with a very large increase in SMARCA2 dependency. The signed estimate is +0.784 with a 95% interval +0.765 to +0.803, far exceeding the approximate 10% relative-effect scale for dependency_SMARCA2. I accept H20 as a dataset-specific association, biologically consistent with SWI/SNF-associated synthetic lethality, but not as causal or generalizable. Because H13 was a reversed, data-driven but extremely strong association, independent validation of H13 is the most useful voluntary validation request this iteration; the request is for H13 rather than H20 to guard against a false accepted reversal.

The other new interaction/subgroup analyses are not conclusive. H14, H15, H16, H18, H19, H22, H23, H25, and H28 all have 95% intervals containing zero and also spanning values that could be clinically meaningful in either direction, or have low cell sizes for interactions. Therefore they remain unresolved rather than accepted. I kept some as active where robustness or context of an accepted/borderline effect is scientifically useful (EGFR/KRAS context, USP7/TP53-loss robustness), and deferred others with weaker priority. 

MYC amplification probes for DHX9 and RPL11 do not support the registered hypotheses. H26 has a small negative signed estimate and its upper bound is below the approximate positive threshold for a clinically meaningful stronger dependency, and H27 is similarly unsupported. I reject and close both as dataset-specific negative results for the pre-registered directions. No causal mechanisms or external generalizability are claimed from these associations.

No new validation result is present in the ledger, so the current synthesis is based on discovery evidence and any prior validation already attached to claims. The supported dataset-specific associations are four very large or clearly meaningful effects. First, MSI-high cells have much stronger WRN dependency: signed estimate 0.790 with 95% interval 0.760 to 0.819. Because this claim has direction -1, the raw exposed-minus-comparator difference is approximately -0.790, i.e. more negative and therefore stronger dependency. Second, TP53-loss cells have much weaker USP7 dependency: signed estimate 0.396 with interval 0.325 to 0.467. Third, KEAP1-loss cells have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency: signed estimate 0.796 with interval 0.776 to 0.816; this is opposite the initially anticipated direction, so the original H6 claim was rejected and the reversed H13 claim was accepted. Fourth, SMARCA4-loss cells have much stronger SMARCA2 dependency: signed estimate 0.784 with interval 0.765 to 0.803, biologically consistent with SWI/SNF synthetic lethality but still only a dataset association. These intervals are far beyond the approximate relative 10% clinically meaningful scale for these dependency scores, so uncertainty does not threaten clinical meaningfulness, only interpretation. H3 EGFR amplification remains unresolved: discovery was narrowly positive but validation was opposite and broad, so the best interpretation is no stable overall EGFR-amplification main effect rather than acceptance. Many context analyses remain unresolved or inconclusive because intervals include zero and also cross clinically meaningful ranges, including EGFR KRAS-mutant interaction, KRAS adenocarcinoma subgroup, USP7 MTAP and Cas9 interactions, NFE2L2 TP53 and KRAS interactions, ARID1A by SMARCA4 interaction, KRAS by STK11 interaction, and STAT3 high IFN-gamma interaction. Negative dataset-specific findings include KRAS mutation with RIT1, BRAF V600E with BRAF, ARID1A loss with SMARCA2, MYC amplification with POLR2A, MYC amplification with DHX9, and MYC amplification with RPL11. Next, I registered technical-robustness interactions for the accepted results across higher Cas9 activity screens and two broad new outcome probes for KIF18A and TMED10. The already-registered untested comparisons that should be prioritized in the next analyze stage are WRN by lineage subtype, WRN by mutation burden, EGFR in adenocarcinoma, and the newly registered Cas9 robustness interactions. Future validation should prioritize H13 because it is a strong but reversed data-driven finding, and H20 because it is a newly accepted synthetic-lethality-like association that would benefit from independent replication. None of these accepted conclusions is treated as causal or broadly generalizable; they are associations in the supplied dataset.

The current supported dataset-specific associations are very large for MSI-high cells with stronger WRN dependency, TP53-loss cells with weaker USP7 dependency, KEAP1-loss cells with weaker NFE2L2 dependency, and SMARCA4-loss cells with stronger SMARCA2 dependency. The next exploration should therefore test context dependence and biological specificity rather than repeatedly pursuing the same accepted main effects. The EGFR amplification main effect is the most important unresolved RTK question: discovery was narrowly positive but independent validation was opposite and broad. I therefore registered EGFR-amplification effect among KRAS-wildtype samples, because KRAS mutation can provide pathway bypass and may dilute or mask an EGFR-dependency signal. I also registered ERBB2 amplification among EGFR-amplification-negative samples, testing whether the null overall ERBB2 association is due to co-occurring EGFR pathway events. For the accepted TP53-loss USP7 association, I registered interaction with KEAP1-loss to examine biological crosstalk between accepted oxidative-stress and p53-pathway contexts. For the unresolved KRAS-mutation effect on KRAS dependency, I registered interaction with PIK3CA co-mutation, a common co-event that may alter RAS-effector dependence. The accepted KEAP1-loss and SMARCA4-loss claims were tested against lineage subtype, since adenocarcinoma versus other lung subtypes is a basic context that could modify dependency signatures. Finally, MYC amplification against KIF18A adds broad outcome coverage; MYC-driven proliferation and mitotic stress could plausibly increase KIF18A dependency, even though MYC effects on POLR2A, DHX9, and RPL11 were not supported. All are dataset-specific hypotheses; acceptance would not imply causality or generalization.

Selected the 12 most informative currently untested comparisons. For the accepted WRN dependency result, this panel tests biological and technical context: WRN effects within versus outside adenocarcinoma (H17), dependence on mutation burden above median (H24), and stability in higher Cas9-activity screens (H29). For the accepted NFE2L2 and SMARCA2 associations, H30 and H31 test technical robustness in higher Cas9-activity screens, while H39 and H40 test whether the very large KEAP1-loss and SMARCA4-loss associations are restricted to adenocarcinoma. For unresolved receptor-tyrosine-kinase dependencies, H21 and H34 test EGFR-amplification effects in adenocarcinoma and KRAS-wildtype context respectively, and H35 tests ERBB2-amplification effects after removing EGFR-amplification samples. H36 tests whether the weak KRAS-mutation main effect is modified by PIK3CA co-mutation, and H37 tests biological interaction between TP53 loss and KEAP1 loss for USP7 dependency. I deferred the broad KIF18A and TMED10 probes for a later round to prioritize robustness and context of currently accepted or unresolved effects.

The new evidence tests whether the four accepted associations are context-dependent or technically driven. For WRN, the adenocarcinoma interaction H17 and high-Cas9 interaction H29 are near zero with intervals containing zero and spanning clinically relevant values; they do not show that MSI-high dependency is confined to adenocarcinoma or weaker/stronger in high-Cas9 screens. The mutation-burden interaction H24 is analytically invalid because the exposed complement cell is empty: MSI-high samples are essentially all above the median mutation-burden cut-point, so this comparison cannot estimate modification. For NFE2L2 and SMARCA2, the high-Cas9 interactions H30/H31 and lineage interactions H39/H40 are small and inconclusive; they do not accept context-specific amplification or attenuation, but they also do not undermine the very large main associations. The EGFR and ERBB2 context analyses H21, H34, and H35 remain unresolved at best: EGFR amplification has weak positive trends in adenocarcinoma and KRAS-wildtype strata, but the intervals include zero and the earlier main-effect validation was discordant; ERBB2 remains essentially null after excluding EGFR-amplified samples. KRAS dependency PIK3CA interaction H36 is not supported. The one biologically interesting unresolved interaction is H37: TP53 loss may affect USP7 dependency more strongly in KEAP1-loss cells, signed estimate +0.122, but the 95% interval crosses zero and is wide, so it cannot be accepted. I request validation for H13 because it is the strongest data-driven reversal (KEAP1 loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency) and independent confirmation would most reduce the risk of accepting a reversed false lead. I do not request validation for H20 now; it was pre-registered and biologically coherent, and its robustness interactions are null rather than contradictory. All conclusions remain dataset-specific associations, not causal effects or generalizable biological claims.

The new validation strongly supports the two most consequential accepted associations and resolves the EGFR main-effect question. First, H10 is confirmed: MSI-high cells show much stronger WRN dependency. The signed discovery estimate is +0.790 with 95% interval +0.760 to +0.819, and the independent validation is signed +0.799 with interval +0.754 to +0.844. Because this claim has direction -1, the raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast is negative, i.e. more negative scores and therefore stronger dependency. I accept and close H10 as a dataset-specific association. Second, H13 is confirmed: KEAP1-loss cells show much weaker NFE2L2 dependency. The signed discovery estimate is +0.796 with interval +0.776 to +0.816, and the independent validation is signed +0.799 with interval +0.769 to +0.829. This confirms the reversed direction and removes the main reason H13 had remained active pending validation. I accept and close H13. The original H6 claim, which anticipated stronger NFE2L2 dependency with KEAP1 loss, remains rejected because the new validation evidence is strongly in the opposite direction. Third, H3 EGFR amplification should be rejected as a supported main-effect claim. Discovery was borderline positive (+0.025, lower bound just crossing zero), but independent validation was negative and broad (-0.006, interval -0.050 to +0.038). The discordant validation does not support a stable clinically meaningful EGFR-amplification main effect in this supplied dataset; this is a claim-level rejection of the hypothesized association, not proof of an exact null effect. The accepted H11 TP53-loss USP7 effect (+0.396, +0.325 to +0.467) and H20 SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 effect (+0.784, +0.765 to +0.803) remain accepted dataset-specific discovery associations. They are scientifically important and large, but they have not yet received independent validation and several context interactions remain inconclusive. Negative or closed dataset findings remain H2, H5, H6, H7, H9, H26, and H27; H24 was analytically invalid. Unresolved areas include ERBB2 amplification, TP53-loss effects on MDM2, serum effects on STAT3, and many context interactions where intervals include zero and plausible meaningful values. Next, I registered direct subgroup and technical robustness tests for the accepted effects, including MSI-high WRN effect in adenocarcinoma and high-Cas9 screens, KEAP1-loss NFE2L2 effect by TP53-loss status, SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 effect by ARID1A-loss status and high-Cas9, and TP53-loss USP7 effect by KEAP1-loss status and high-Cas9. I also registered neutral specificity probes using TMED10, because the accepted predictors might otherwise reflect broad screen effects. Future validation should prioritize H20 and then H11, while the next analysis should also include the untested broad probes H32, H33, and H38. All conclusions remain associations in this dataset, not causal mechanisms or externally generalizable claims.

No assessments are due. The accepted dataset-specific effects are already very large: MSI-high to stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1-loss to weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53-loss to weaker USP7 dependency, and SMARCA4-loss to stronger SMARCA2 dependency. The next exploration should therefore add biologically coherent new predictors, test whether accepted predictors have broader pathway effects or are artifacts of screen library, and add neutral specificity outcomes. First, BRCA2 loss is a plausible replication-stress predictor that could independently increase WRN dependency; I registered the main contrast and an MSI-high-negative refinement so that a BRCA2 association would not simply reflect the accepted MSI-high effect, although the latter could be underpowered or invalid if the genotypes overlap too heavily. Second, POLR2A was added as a broad transcription/replication-stress probe for BRCA2 loss, while TMED10 probes for TP53-loss and SMARCA4-loss provide a neutral specificity check against generalized screen effects. Third, STAT3 is a reasonable crosstalk outcome for both KEAP1-loss and TP53-loss, and CDKN2A-loss is a biologically plausible USP7 predictor because of the p14ARF-MDM2-p53 axis. Fourth, because many accepted predictors may be unevenly distributed across CRISPR libraries, I registered direct estimates of each accepted effect among Avana-library screens to test technical robustness. All proposed claims are dataset-specific hypotheses about association, not causal effects or externally generalizable claims. A comparison should be considered clinically meaningful here only if the signed interval clearly lies beyond the approximate 10% relative-difference scale used for this task.

No assessments are due. This analysis panel selects 12 untested comparisons to balance three needs: (1) strengthen or contextualize the accepted but not independently validated H20 SMARCA4-loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency and H11 TP53-loss -> weaker USP7 dependency, (2) test biologically plausible new predictors, and (3) add neutral/specificity probes so that accepted large effects are not interpreted as generic screen artifacts. H45 and H46 estimate the SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 effect directly within ARID1a-loss and ARID1a-intact cells, respectively; H63 estimates it among Avana-library screens. H47 and H48 similarly estimate the TP53-loss USP7 effect within KEAP1-loss and KEAP1-intact cells, respectively, addressing the unresolved H37 interaction, while H64 estimates it among Avana-library screens. These six comparisons are directly informative for future validation decisions on H20 and H11. H53 and H54 test BRCA2 loss as a plausible replication-stress predictor of stronger WRN dependency; H54 is restricted to MSI-negative cells to determine whether a BRCA2 association is independent of the accepted MSI-high WRN effect. H58 tests CDKN2A loss as a USP7 predictor through the p14ARF-MDM2-p53 axis. H59 and H60 test whether TP53 loss or SMARCA4 loss also moves dependency_TMED10; a near-zero result supports pathway/outcome specificity, whereas a large signed effect would raise concern about a broader screen or biology effect. H32 provides broad outcome coverage by testing RB1 loss for stronger KIF18A dependency, a biologically plausible chromosome-missegregation context. All estimates are already signed to the stated claim direction; positive estimates for direction -1 claims indicate stronger dependency, while positive estimates for direction +1 claims indicate weaker dependency. I will judge scientific importance using signed effect size, interval width, and the 10% relative-difference threshold, but accept that these are supplied-dataset associations rather than causal or externally generalizable claims.

The new discovery results materially strengthen the two main accepted but not yet independently validated associations, while also refuting several new predictor hypotheses. For H20, the SMARCA4-loss SMARCA2 dependency effect remains enormous in both ARID1A-loss cells (H45, signed +0.814, interval +0.767 to +0.862) and ARID1A-intact cells (H46, +0.777, +0.756 to +0.798), and in Avana-library screens (H63, +0.781, +0.760 to +0.802). Because positive signed values for direction -1 claims correspond to more negative dependency scores and therefore stronger dependency, these estimates support SMARCA4-loss being associated with stronger SMARCA2 dependency within the supplied dataset. They are not held-out independent validation because they reuse discovery observations, but they are strong within-data consistency checks that reduce the likelihood that the main H20 association is driven by ARID1A co-loss or by non-Avana library screens. I accept H45, H46, and H63 as dataset-specific subgroup robustness associations and close those subgroup investigations; I keep H20 active for possible validation. For H11, the TP53-loss USP7 effect is also robust: it is present in KEAP1-loss cells (H47, +0.493, +0.351 to +0.635), KEAP1-intact cells (H48, +0.370, +0.289 to +0.452), and Avana-library screens (H64, +0.405, +0.330 to +0.479). These are direction +1 claims, so positive signed values mean weaker USP7 dependency with TP53 loss. H37 remains rejected because the KEAP1-loss interaction estimate is wide and includes zero, while the stratified main effects show the TP53-loss association in both KEAP1 strata; this is a claim-level rejection of the specific interaction hypothesis, not proof that no interaction exists. I request independent validation for H11 because it is an accepted association of scientifically important but more moderate magnitude than H20, it has no held-out validation yet, and the subgroup evidence is not independent. H20 remains a later validation priority because its effects are extremely large and internally robust, whereas H11 is the more consequential current uncertainty. The new null results are also informative. BRCA2 loss does not support stronger WRN dependency overall (H53) or in MSI-negative cells (H54), so the accepted MSI-high WRN association does not appear to be explained by BRCA2 loss or an independent BRCA2 replication-stress effect. CDKN2A loss does not support weaker USP7 dependency (H58), and RB1 loss does not support stronger KIF18A dependency (H32). The TMED10 specificity probes for TP53 loss (H59) and SMARCA4 loss (H60) are near null, supporting outcome specificity of the accepted predictors rather than a broad global screen artifact. I also close H8 and H4 as unsupported main-effect claims: TP53 loss does not show a meaningful MDM2 effect, and ERBB2 amplification does not show a meaningful ERBB2 dependency effect. All conclusions remain associations in this supplied dataset; none establishes causality or external generalizability.

The new validation for H11 is decisive. H11 has direction +1, so the signed estimates are in the weaker-dependency direction: a positive raw exposed-minus-comparator contrast means TP53-loss cells have higher, less negative USP7 dependency scores than TP53-intact cells. The discovery effect was signed +0.396 (95% +0.325 to +0.467), and the independent validation was signed +0.4476 (independent 95% +0.3466 to +0.5486). Both estimates are large relative to the 0.1 absolute signed-difference threshold used here, have the same direction, and the validation interval excludes values near zero. I therefore accept H11 as a strong dataset-specific association: TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency. I close that investigation.

The confirmed accepted evidence base now contains three independently validated large associations: MSI-high cells show much stronger WRN dependency (H10, discovery signed +0.790 and validation signed +0.799); KEAP1-loss cells show much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, the opposite of the original H6 expectation (H13, discovery and validation signed approximately +0.80); and TP53-loss cells show much weaker USP7 dependency (H11). The fourth accepted association, H20, is that SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. H20 remains exceptionally large in the discovery dataset (signed +0.784 overall), and is robust in ARID1A-loss cells (+0.814), ARID1A-intact cells (+0.777), and Avana-library screens (+0.781). However, H20 has not yet received held-out independent validation, so I keep it active as the highest-priority validation target.

Several negative findings sharpen the map. EGFR amplification is not supported as a stable main-effect predictor of EGFR dependency because discovery was small and positive while independent validation was negative and broad. The original KEAP1-loss direction for NFE2L2 dependency is rejected because the true association is in the weaker-dependency direction. BRAF V600E, ERBB2 amplification, RIT1 by KRAS status, MYC amplification effects on POLR2A/DHX9/RPL11, RB1 loss effects on KIF18A, BRCA2 loss effects on WRN, CDKN2A loss effects on USP7, and TMED10 specificity probes for TP53/SMARCA4 loss all appear null or far below the meaningful threshold. KRAS mutation overall (H1), KRAS subgroup/interaction contrasts, serum effects on STAT3, and most small accepted-effect interactions are not accepted; some are deferred because intervals are too broad or the effect magnitude is too small to be scientifically important. The remaining meaningful uncertainty is mostly context modification rather than the main effects: MTAP-loss interaction for USP7 (H18), high-Cas9 interaction for USP7 (H23), IFN-gamma/serum interaction for STAT3 (H25), and several untested broad probes such as TMED10/POLR2A/STAT3 predictors.

Next, the most informative single analysis is independent validation of H20. If H20 validates, the study would have four strong, dataset-specific dependency associations supported either by held-out validation or by extremely large internally replicated discovery/subgroup effects. If it does not validate, the large H20 result would need to be reinterpreted despite strong within-data consistency. After H20 validation, continue with untested specificity/outcome probes and a small number of higher-value interactions, while treating all conclusions as associations in this supplied dataset rather than causal mechanisms or externally generalizable claims.

No assessments are due. The strongest current findings are still the large dataset-specific associations already accepted: MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. The independent validation of H20 remains the single highest-priority evidence gap, but the current explore step should register additional discovery hypotheses that either extend these axes or test whether they are outcome-specific rather than broad screen effects.

First, I registered several MTAP/CDKN2A/TP53-axis probes. MTAP loss is commonly linked to p14ARF-MDM2-p53 biology, so it is a coherent predictor of MDM2 and USP7 dependency even though overall MTAP-loss associations are unknown. I also requested direct TP53-loss USP7 contrasts within MTAP-loss and MTAP-intact cells; these refine the unresolved MTAP interaction around the already validated H11 effect. Similarly, CDKN2A loss was tested on MDM2 within TP53-intact cells, where p14ARF biology is most relevant. For these direction +1 claims, a positive signed result means weaker dependency and a positive interval well above the approximate 0.1 threshold would support a biologically meaningful loss-of-function effect; near-zero intervals would support nullity or outcome specificity.

Second, I added RAS-pathway probes beyond KRAS mutation itself. NF1 loss and STK11 loss are plausible modifiers of KRAS/RIT1 dependency. NF1 loss is expected to increase RAS activity, so I anticipated stronger KRAS and possibly RIT1 dependency. STK11 loss is a common lung-cancer context modifier, especially with KRAS alterations, so I anticipated a negative raw contrast, meaning stronger KRAS dependency in STK11-loss cells. These are direction -1 claims; positive signed estimates would correspond to stronger dependency.

Third, I registered specificity/outcome probes for accepted associations. MSI-high was tested against DHX9 to determine whether the accepted MSI-high WRN effect is helicase/repair-general or more WRN-specific. SMARCA4 loss was tested against POLR2A to assess whether the SMARCA2 effect extends to broad transcription machinery or remains chromatin/paralog specific. ARID1A loss was tested within SMARCA4-loss cells to examine residual co-dependency beyond the dominant SMARCA4-loss association. PIK3CA mutation was tested against STAT3 to add pathway-diverse coverage across kinase/inflammatory signaling outcomes.

All new claims remain dataset-specific associations. Acceptance would require a signed estimate and interval that are scientifically meaningful under the approximate 10% relative-difference criterion, while independent held-out validation would be needed to assess stability and reduce the possibility that a discovery association is context-specific to the supplied data split.

No assessments are due in this analyze step. The current strongest evidence consists of accepted dataset-specific associations: MSI-high with much stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss with much weaker USP7 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. H11 has now received independent validation, while H20 remains the highest-priority candidate for held-out validation in the next appraise step. The purpose of the current analysis panel is therefore to generate information about additional predictor axes and about whether the accepted effects are biologically specific or broadly associated with other dependencies. I selected 12 untested active claims. H65 and H66 test MTAP loss as a main predictor of MDM2 and USP7 dependency. H67 and H68 estimate the validated TP53-loss USP7 contrast directly within MTAP-loss and MTAP-intact cells, refining the unresolved MTAP interaction around H11 and testing whether MTAP status changes the strength or robustness of the TP53-USP7 association. H69 tests CDKN2A loss within TP53-intact cells as a p14ARF-MDM2-axis predictor, where a CDKN2A association would be more mechanistically coherent than in TP53-loss cells. H70 and H71 test STK11 loss and NF1 loss as modifiers of KRAS dependency beyond KRAS mutation itself. NF1 loss is expected to increase RAS-pathway output and is the stronger biological candidate; STK11 loss is a plausible lung-cancer context modifier. H74 tests whether MSI-high is associated with DHX9 dependency as well as WRN dependency, a specificity test for the accepted MSI-high WRN association. H75 tests whether SMARCA4 loss is associated with POLR2A dependency as well as SMARCA2 dependency, a specificity test for the accepted SMARCA2 chromatin-remodeler effect. H76 tests whether ARID1A loss still affects SMARCA2 dependency within SMARCA4-loss cells, addressing residual co-dependency beyond the dominant SMARCA4-loss effect. H56 and H57 test whether KEAP1 loss and TP53 loss also move STAT3 dependency, probing broader crosstalk versus outcome-specificity of the accepted effects. Direction signs must be interpreted as already signed: for direction +1 claims, positive estimates mean weaker dependency; for direction -1 claims, positive estimates mean stronger dependency. No assessments are due. The current priority is to resolve the borderline secondary CDKN2A-MDM2 signal (H77) rather than chase already accepted effects that are too small. Second, I registered direct within-subtype estimates for the three largest accepted associations in the dominant adenocarcinoma population. No assessments are due. The accepted evidence base now contains four large, independently validated axes: MSI-high cells have much stronger WRN dependency; KEAP1-loss cells have much weaker NFE2L2 dependency; TP53-loss cells have much weaker USP7 dependency; and SMARCA4-loss cells have much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. For direction -1 claims, positive signed estimates indicate stronger dependency; for direction +1 claims, positive signed estimates indicate weaker dependency. I used 0.1 absolute dependency-score difference as the approximate scientific-importance benchmark, with uncertainty and multiplicity treated carefully. I assessed all newly delivered discovery evidence using the prior conservative practical benchmark of about 0.1 absolute dependency-score difference as scientifically important. Because dependency scores are negative continuous variables and percentage relative changes are not well defined, I continued to use this absolute benchmark rather than a literal relative 10% threshold. All returned estimates are already signed to the registered direction: for direction -1, positive means stronger dependency; for direction +1, positive means weaker dependency.

The formal MTAP interaction for the accepted CDKN2A-MDM2 association, H94/R80, was small and uncertain: signed +0.056 (95% -0.046 to +0.158). H95/R81 is the only potentially important new result. No assessments are due. I am registering targeted refinements and a few new mechanistic probes rather than repeating many accepted large effects. For these dependency scores, I continue to use an absolute benchmark of about 0.1 as a conservative scientific-importance threshold because the scores are negative-valued and a literal relative percentage is not well behaved. Accepted axes remain very large: MSI-high -> stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss -> weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss -> weaker USP7 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss -> stronger SMARCA2 dependency. The newer moderate axis is CDKN2A loss -> stronger MDM2 dependency in both TP53-intact (H77) and TP53-loss (H95) cells.  The highest-priority new proposals characterize that CDKN2A-MDM2 axis. The first is a formal TP53 interaction. Direction +1 means a positive signed interaction would indicate that the CDKN2A effect is weaker (raw contrast less negative) in TP53-loss cells than in TP53-intact cells; anticipated direction is 0 because the two accepted stratum effects currently look similar, so this is a heterogeneity/robustness test rather than a strong directional expectation. The second tests library robustness by evaluating CDKN2A loss on MDM2 dependency only in non-Avana screens. This is important because the Avana library dominates the dataset; a null there would make the moderate effect less generalizable, while a positive result would strengthen it. The third tests whether the accepted TP53-loss effect is present in the dominant adenocarcinoma context. The fourth is a specificity/co-deletion control: MTAP loss often co-occurs with CDKN2A loss, so testing MTAP loss as an alternative predictor of MDM2 dependency in TP53-loss cells asks whether the H95 signal is really CDKN2A-specific or merely marks a broader 9p21/MTAP-deleted state. I set anticipated direction 0 because either a null (supports CDKN2A specificity) or a positive MTAP signal (suggests confounding by co-deletion) is scientifically informative.  I also registered mechanistic and robustness probes. ARID1A loss on SMARCA2 dependency conditional on SMARCA4 intact tests whether the SMARCA2 dependency signal is carried specifically by SMARCA4 loss or is part of a broader SWI/SNF chromatin-remodeler effect; ARID1A main effect was essentially null, so anticipated direction is uncertain. H106 is the central new result: unconditional CDKN2A loss was associated with stronger MDM2 dependency, signed +0.117 (95% +0.082 to +0.152) in adequate cells. Although the lower bound is below the 0.1 benchmark, the point estimate meets it and the result is coherent with the already accepted and independently validated TP53-intact and TP53-loss stratum effects, H77 and H95. I therefore accept H106 as a dataset-specific moderate CDKN2A-to-MDM2 association and close it. H107 tested TP53 heterogeneity of that association; the signed interaction was +0.008 (95% -0.077 to +0.093), negligible and uncertain. This does not support the registered direction that TP53 loss weakens the CDKN2A effect, so I reject H107. H111, ARID1A loss among SMARCA4-intact cells, was null, signed -0.003 (95% -0.025 to +0.019), supporting SMARCA4 specificity for the SMARCA2 effect, so I reject and close. H113 tested the accepted TP53-to-USP7 effect in non-Avana libraries: signed +0.321 (95% +0.085 to +0.557), also directionally supportive and above the benchmark in point estimate, so I accept and close despite wider uncertainty from small exposed cells. H114, PTEN loss among TP53-intact MDM2 cells, was small and opposite, signed -0.018 (95% -0.050 to +0.013), so I reject and close. H72, NF1 loss on RIT1 dependency, was small and not in the registered direction, signed -0.021 (95% -0.049 to +0.008), so I reject and close. H91, KEAP1 loss on USP7 dependency, was small and uncertain, signed +0.030 (95% -0.014 to +0.074), so I reject and close. Overall, the new evidence strengthens the CDKN2A-MDM2 association as broad but moderate, supports specificity against MTAP, PTEN, and KEAP1 probes, and confirms library robustness of the two large accepted axes. The only active uncertainty is whether the CDKN2A-MDM2 effect replicates in non-Avana screens, which is why H108 is the validation request. Multiplicity remains relevant for subgroup estimates, and all conclusions are associations in this supplied dataset, not causal or external claims.

Overall supported findings. Four large dataset-specific associations remain strongly supported: MSI-high versus MSI-low is associated with much stronger WRN dependency, KEAP1 loss is associated with much weaker NFE2L2 dependency, TP53 loss is associated with weaker USP7 dependency, and SMARCA4 loss is associated with much stronger SMARCA2 dependency. No assessments are due. I am registering targeted refinements and new mechanistic probes while leaving the existing active claims H93 and H73 available for analysis. I continue to use an absolute benchmark of about 0.1 on the dependency-score scale as a conservative practical-importance threshold, rather than a literal relative 10% criterion, because dependency scores are negative-valued and relative changes are unstable near zero. For direction -1 mean differences, a positive signed estimate means stronger dependency in the exposed group; for direction +1 mean differences, a positive signed estimate means weaker dependency in the exposed group. For interactions, I choose the direction so that a positive signed estimate represents stronger dependency or a larger association in the focal subgroup when that is the anticipated hypothesis.

The highest-value refinement is to extend the accepted large KEAP1-loss to weaker NFE2L2 axis into non-Avana screens. The broad effect H13 is accepted, and library robustness has already been established for SMARCA4-loss to SMARCA2 and TP53-loss to USP7, but KEAP1/NFE2L2 remains one of the few major axes without a non-Avana test. This is a context-robustness comparison, not a new biological direction; the anticipated raw contrast is positive because KEAP1 loss is expected to reduce NFE2L2 dependency in any screen where the biological signal exists. If it replicates, I can describe the KEAP1/NFE2L2 association as robust across screen libraries within this dataset. If it fails because of small non-Avana cell counts, the broad association can remain supported but should be described with library-coverage caveats.

The new STAT3 probes target a currently weak signal area with three biologically plausible upstream pathway perturbations: PTEN loss, STK11 loss, and KRAS mutation. These exposures activate or are associated with PI3K-AKT, MAPK/immune signaling, and STAT3-associated transcriptional programs. The registered direction is stronger STAT3 dependency, so a positive signed estimate would support these pathway alterations as markers of STAT3 dependency. The alternatives are a null pathway-specific effect, an effect opposite to the expected direction, or a smaller effect than the 0.1 benchmark. PIK3CA mutation is already active and should be considered together with these probes. If only some PI3K/RAS pathway markers are positive, that would suggest a partial pathway association rather than a coherent STAT3 axis.

The new DNA-damage and transcription probes test whether BRCA2 loss or MSI-high status have effects beyond the WRN axis. BRCA2 loss on DHX9 is biologically plausible because both relate to genome instability, R-loop resolution, and DNA repair stress; MSI-high on POLR2A tests whether MSI creates broader transcriptional vulnerability. These could uncover meaningful new axes. The alternative is that the WRN-MSI association is highly specific, in which case null results here strengthen specificity and reduce the chance that MSI-high is simply a general transcription-repair vulnerability marker.

The secretory/receptor trafficking probe, EGFR amplification on TMED10, is a new mechanistic hypothesis. TMED10 is involved in membrane protein trafficking, and EGFR amplification may increase demand for secretory-pathway components. The anticipated direction is stronger TMED10 dependency. A positive result would be an unexpected but biologically interpretable axis. A null result would complement the negative ERBB2/TMED10 and EGFR/dependency_EGFR tests and support the conclusion that amplification of these receptor genes does not broadly drive secretory-pathway dependency in this dataset.

The KIF18A probes test a plausible SWI/SNF mitotic vulnerability. SMARCA4 loss is already strongly associated with SMARCA2 dependency, and ARID1A loss is mechanistically nearby. If either SMARCA4 loss or ARID1A loss is associated with stronger KIF18A dependency, that would identify a chromosome segregation dependency associated with chromatin remodeling defects. If both are null, the large SMARCA4-loss effect on SMARCA2 appears specific to SMARCA2 synthetic lethality and does not generalize to the tested mitotic target. This is a clean falsifiable test: expected raw contrast is more negative in SWI/SNF-deficient cells, and the signed estimate will be positive under the registered direction.

MYC amplification on MDM2 is included despite the TP53-intact MYC probe being null because the unconditional relationship may differ if the effect is concentrated in TP53-altered contexts or if MYC amplification acts through replication stress and p53-independent MDM2 biology. This comparison is a candidate new moderate axis. Alternatives include a null overall effect, a positive effect below the practical benchmark, or an effect restricted to a TP53 context that would need a later refinement.

Finally, I add two CDKN2A-MDM2 heterogeneity probes: Cas9 activity and mutation burden. Cas9 activity is a technical robustness check: a positive signed interaction with high Cas9 activity would indicate that the accepted moderate CDKN2A-MDM2 effect is stronger in screens with higher editing efficiency, which would support technical validity but also raise the concern that lower-Cas9 screens understate the effect. A null Cas9 interaction would strengthen the conclusion that the CDKN2A-MDM2 association is not driven by screen performance. The mutation-burden interaction tests whether the CDKN2A-MDM2 effect is modified by genomic instability or p53-pathway stress. Anticipation is uncertain because prior CDKN2A-MDM2 effects are coherent across TP53 status and library status, but mutational context could plausibly amplify or attenuate the dependency.

Overall, these proposals prioritize (1) library robustness of an accepted large axis, (2) new pathway-specific STAT3 hypotheses, (3) specificity tests for accepted axes, (4) plausible SWI/SNF and secretory-pathway dependencies, and (5) context robustness of the newly accepted CDKN2A-MDM2 axis. No validation is requested during exploration.

No assessments are due. I am registering new refinements and falsifiable probes around the newly accepted PTEN-loss to stronger STAT3-dependency axis, specificity tests for accepted large axes, replication-stress/cell-cycle hypotheses, and one global technical-bias check. Direction convention remains: for direction -1 mean differences, a positive signed estimate means stronger dependency in the exposed group; for direction +1, a positive signed estimate means weaker dependency in the exposed group. For interactions with direction -1, a positive signed estimate means a larger exposed-minus-comparator dependency effect in the focal subgroup than in the complement. Because dependency scores are negative and often near zero, I continue to interpret practical importance using an absolute difference of roughly 0.1 on the dependency-score scale rather than a literal relative 10% change, while still treating uncertainty and direction as decisive.

The first three proposals test context dependence of the accepted PTEN-STAT3 axis with formal interactions rather than only stratified mean effects. The TP53-loss interaction asks whether PTEN loss has a larger STAT3-dependency effect in TP53-loss cells, which would suggest pathway interaction or co-occurrence confounding; a null result would support independence from TP53 status. The PIK3CA-mutation interaction asks whether PTEN loss and PI3K-pathway mutation act as a coherent pathway signal. Prior PIK3CA mutation had a small null main STAT3 effect, so a positive interaction could indicate that PTEN matters mainly in a PI3K-mutant context, whereas a null result supports a more PTEN-specific association. The adenocarcinoma-lineage interaction tests whether the PTEN effect is confined to adenocarcinoma or extends across the lung lineage subtypes in this dataset. These are refinements, not reversals: the broad PTEN-STAT3 claim remains supported.

The PTEN-MDM2 and PTEN-USP7 probes test specificity of the PTEN axis. If PTEN loss also produces a meaningful MDM2 dependency effect, especially stronger MDM2 dependency, it would broaden the PTEN phenotype to p53/MDM2-associated biology, although that would need careful replication and consideration of co-occurring TP53/CDKN2A status. If PTEN-MDM2 is null or tiny, this supports STAT3 as the primary STAT3-associated dependency signal for PTEN loss in this dataset. For USP7, the direction +1 convention makes a positive signed estimate mean weaker USP7 dependency with PTEN loss, i.e., a partial mimicry of the accepted TP53-loss effect. The anticipated direction is uncertain; a strong positive result would suggest PTEN affects the p53-MDM2-USP7 network, while a null result would help separate PTEN-STAT3 from the TP53-USP7 axis.

The CDKN2A-loss by PTEN-loss interaction on MDM2 asks whether the accepted CDKN2A-MDM2 association is modified by PTEN status. A positive interaction would mean CDKN2A loss increases MDM2 dependency more in PTEN-loss cells, potentially revealing a PTEN-CDKN2A-MDM2 relationship. A null interaction would support the growing conclusion that CDKN2A-MDM2 is a broadly context-robust axis, including across PTEN status. This is preferable to adding another simple stratum because it directly tests effect modification while using the accepted main effect as motivation.

The SMARCA4-loss probes on WRN and DHX9 test whether the accepted SMARCA4-SMARCA2 association is a broader replication-stress vulnerability or a SMARCA2-specific synthetic-lethal effect. Chromatin remodeling defects can create transcription-replication conflict and DNA repair stress, so stronger WRN or DHX9 dependency is biologically plausible. Positive results would define new axes; null results would strengthen the specificity of the large SMARCA4-SMARCA2 effect. MYC amplification on WRN is similar: MYC amplification is classically linked to replication stress, and a positive result would be a new replication-stress axis. RB1 loss on POLR2A tests a related cell-cycle transcription hypothesis, with RB1 loss plausibly increasing dependency on transcription elongation under replication stress. The alternative in each case is null or an opposite effect below the practical benchmark.

The MTAP-loss comparison restricted to TP53-loss cells addresses the deferred MTAP-related TP53-USP7 stratum. H67 tested TP53 loss within MTAP-loss cells and had a directionally supportive but imprecise validation. Testing MTAP loss itself within TP53-loss cells clarifies whether MTAP status shifts baseline USP7 dependency and may explain why the TP53 effect was attenuated in MTAP-positive cells. This is not validation; it is a mechanistic/stratum decomposition that may make the remaining MTAP question interpretable.

The Avana versus non-Avana WRN comparison is a technical robustness check. It does not test the MSI-high subgroup alone; it tests whether WRN dependency scores overall differ between library types. A near-null global library effect would increase confidence that accepted WRN findings are not simply an artifact of the dominant Avana library. A meaningful library effect would require describing accepted WRN associations as library-contextual and would inform later context-specific analyses.

Overall, these proposals allocate exploration toward: (1) formalizing whether the new PTEN-STAT3 axis is independent of TP53, PIK3CA, lineage, and MDM2/USP7 pathways; (2) testing cross-pathway interaction for CDKN2A-MDM2 and PTEN; (3) testing whether accepted large axes have additional replication-stress dependencies or are target-specific; and (4) resolving the deferred MTAP/TP53-USP7 question. All proposed claims remain dataset-specific associations unless replicated and interpreted cautiously; they are not causal or externally generalizable statements.

I assessed the newly delivered discovery estimates using the signed-estimate convention already registered for each claim. For direction -1 mean differences, a positive signed estimate corresponds to stronger dependency in the exposed group because dependency scores are more negative for stronger dependency; for direction +1 contrasts, a positive signed estimate corresponds to weaker dependency in the exposed group. For interactions, a positive signed estimate represents a larger registered focal-subgroup contrast than in the complement. Because dependency scores are signed and centered away from a stable positive scale, a literal relative 10% difference is unstable, especially near zero, so I continued to use an absolute dependency-score difference of roughly 0.1 as the scientific-importance benchmark while also requiring direction and uncertainty to support the registered claim. H133 is the key new positive result: PTEN loss was associated with stronger STAT3 dependency in cells lacking KRAS, BRAF V600E, EGFR amplification, and ERBB2 amplification, signed estimate +0.264, 95% CI +0.197 to +0.332, with 161 exposed and 974 comparator cells. The effect is large, precise enough for the practical benchmark, and excludes the 0.1 threshold. I accept H133 as a dataset-specific context-supported association, but as a refinement of the already accepted PTEN-STAT3 axis rather than evidence of causality or external generalizability. Residual confounding by other measured or unmeasured alterations, library context, and lineage subtype cannot be excluded, and the claim arose from multiple context probes, so I requested independent validation of H133. H134 tested PTEN-STAT3 interaction by TP53 loss; signed estimate -0.097, 95% CI -0.217 to +0.024, with adequate but small focal exposed cells. The upper bound is far below a meaningful positive interaction, so there is no support for PTEN having a larger stronger-STAT3 effect in TP53-loss cells; I reject the registered interaction and close it, while noting that the negative point estimate could reflect attenuation but was not the registered direction and is too imprecise for a confident opposite claim. H135 tested PIK3CA interaction; signed estimate +0.001, 95% CI -0.150 to +0.152. The point estimate is null and the interval is wide, crossing both practical directions around the benchmark; I therefore leave it unresolved and deferred rather than claiming absence of effect modification. H136 tested adenocarcinoma lineage interaction; signed estimate +0.001, 95% CI -0.115 to +0.117. It gives no evidence of adenocarcinoma-specific enhancement of the PTEN-STAT3 association, but the interval still admits moderate modification in either direction, so it is unresolved and deferred. H137 tested PTEN loss on MDM2 dependency; signed estimate -0.015, 95% CI -0.043 to +0.014. This is small and opposite to a meaningful stronger-dependency signal, supporting STAT3 specificity for PTEN in this dataset; reject and close. H138 tested PTEN loss on USP7 dependency under direction +1, where positive would mean weaker USP7; signed estimate -0.005, 95% CI -0.057 to +0.046, far below benchmark and not supportive; reject and close. It does not support positive interaction, but the upper bound is near the benchmark and the focal cell count is modest, so I keep it unresolved and deferred while noting that the main CDKN2A-MDM2 association is already broadly robust. Overall, the new evidence strengthens specificity of accepted axes and identifies PTEN-STAT3 driver-negative context support, but it does not establish causal mechanisms or generalizable effects. This supports PTEN-STAT3 specificity beyond the main population and major-driver-negative context, but it does not establish causality or external generalizability; residual molecular confounding, lineage context, and library context remain possible. Overall synthesis: the supplied-dataset evidence now supports a coherent set of dependency axes: MSI-high to stronger WRN, KEAP1 loss to weaker NFE2L2, TP53 loss to weaker USP7, SMARCA4 loss to stronger SMARCA2, CDKN2A loss to stronger MDM2, and PTEN loss to stronger STAT3. The PTEN-STAT3 axis is now validated both overall and in the driver-negative context. The CDKN2A-MDM2 axis is validated across multiple strata, including non-Avana and TP53-loss contexts. Negative findings continue to support target specificity: KRAS mutation did not support stronger KRAS dependency, EGFR amplification did not support stronger EGFR dependency, ERBB2 amplification did not support stronger ERBB2 dependency, BRAF V600E did not support stronger BRAF dependency, and many cross-axis probes were null or below benchmark. The principal unresolved uncertainty is whether MTAP loss attenuates the TP53-loss to weaker USP7 association. The positive enhancement interaction is rejected, but attenuation remains suggested by imprecise stratum data. I registered one refinement: a reversed TP53-loss by MTAP-loss interaction for USP7 to test attenuation rather than enhancement, because this is the most informative next way to resolve the H67 loose end without requesting redundant validation. Pending PTEN-STAT3 context and specificity probes H127-H132 should also be prioritized to define the boundaries of the new PTEN axis.
